# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 25 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 25 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_025_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 5 — The Transition to the Shepherd

**1** The vision of the fifth order that appeared to me, brothers and sisters, is as follows. **2** I was fasting and sitting on a certain mountain, giving thanks to the Lord for all that he had done for me, when I saw the Shepherd sitting beside me, who said: "Why have you come here so early?" I replied, "Because, sir, I keep a station here." **3** He said to me, "I am the angel of repentance. I have been sent to dwell with you for the rest of your life." **4** It seemed to me that he had come to test me. I said to him, "Who are you? For I know to whom I have been entrusted and who it is that dwells with me." He replied, "Do you not recognize me?" "No," I said. He said, "I am the Shepherd to whom you have been entrusted." **5** While he was speaking, his form changed, and I recognized him as the one to whom I had been entrusted. Immediately I was overcome with confusion; fear seized me, and I was overwhelmed with grief that I had spoken to him in such a rude and foolish way. **6** He replied: "Do not be confused, but be strengthened in my commandments which I am about to give you. For I have been sent," he said, "to show you again all that you saw before, and especially those things most important for your life. First of all, keep my commandments and you will be pleasing to God. **7** Write the Commandments and the Parables." **8** When he had finished speaking he rose and departed, and I could not see in which direction he went. There was a noise; I turned and was afraid, thinking it was the beast. But when I looked there was nothing — only the man sitting beside me.

---

### Council Notes

Chapter 25 is the structural hinge of the entire Shepherd of Hermas. The Visions section (chs. 1-25) ends here; the Mandates and Similitudes now follow under the Shepherd's instruction.

The identity of the Shepherd as "the angel of repentance" (ho angelos tēs metanoias) is the book's central theological claim. He is not just a teaching figure but an agent of divine transformation — sent specifically to be Hermas's constant companion and instructor.

The commission "Write the Commandments and the Parables" (v. 7) is the literary self-awareness of the Shepherd — the book explicitly presents itself as a divinely authorized writing project.

The detail that the man was still sitting beside Hermas after the noise (v. 8) — suggesting the Shepherd reappeared instantly — emphasizes his supernatural nature and his permanent presence with Hermas from this point forward.
